title: Insomnia Triples Breast Cancer Risk in Women Under 50. A New Study Just Made Sleep a Cancer Conversation.
excerpt: Research presented at ASCO 2026 found that women diagnosed with insomnia were three times more likely to develop breast cancer within five years. For South Asian women — who face unique sleep pressures — the findings demand attention.
body:
The relationship between poor sleep and poor health has been well established. But a new study presented at the American Society of Clinical Oncology conference in Chicago has drawn a line that is harder to ignore: insomnia may be a direct risk factor for cancer in young adults, and the numbers for women are alarming.

Researchers from Jefferson Health in New Jersey and the Anderson Cancer Centre in New Orleans analyzed health data from 18.9 million people between the ages of 18 and 50, spanning 2021 to 2025. Women who had been diagnosed with insomnia were three times more likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer within the following five years compared to women without the sleep disorder. The risk of uterine cancer was doubled. Ovarian cancer risk was 60 per cent higher. For both men and women, the risk of early-onset colorectal cancer was 85 per cent higher.

## Not a Correlation Story

What makes this study different from the standard "sleep is important" messaging is the specificity and scale. This was not a survey of self-reported sleep habits. It tracked clinically diagnosed insomnia against actual cancer diagnoses across nearly 19 million patient records. The researchers controlled for known cancer risk factors and still found statistically significant associations.

"These findings suggest that sleep disruption may be a clinically relevant, potentially modifiable risk factor in early-onset cancer risk," the authors told the ASCO conference. The key word is "modifiable." Unlike genetic predisposition or family history, sleep is something most people can improve.

The study did find important limits. There was no significant link between insomnia and cancers of the throat, stomach, pancreas, prostate, or testicles. The cancers with the strongest connections — breast, uterine, and ovarian — are closely tied to the hormone oestrogen. Sleep disruption is known to alter oestrogen metabolism, which may explain the mechanism.

## The South Asian Dimension

South Asian women in the United States face a confluence of factors that make these findings especially relevant. Cultural expectations often place women at the centre of household management, childcare, and eldercare — all of which compress sleep windows. First-generation immigrant women frequently maintain two social clocks, managing daytime obligations in America and evening connections with family in India.

A 2023 study published in the Journal of Immigrant and Minority Health found that South Asian immigrant women in the U.S. reported shorter sleep durations and poorer sleep quality than both white American women and South Asian women living in India. The researchers attributed this to acculturative stress, caregiving responsibilities, and social isolation.

Add to this the well-documented reluctance in many South Asian families to treat sleep problems as medical issues. Insomnia is often dismissed as stress or handled with home remedies — warm milk, chamomile, or simply being told to "stop worrying." The result is that clinically significant sleep disorders go undiagnosed and untreated for years, precisely the scenario this study links to elevated cancer risk.

## What the Data Actually Says

The numbers from the ASCO study deserve to be stated plainly:

Breast cancer risk with insomnia: **3x higher** in women under 50. Uterine cancer risk: **2x higher**. Ovarian cancer risk: **60% higher**. Colorectal cancer risk: **85% higher** (both sexes).

These are relative risks, not absolute risks. A threefold increase in a rare event is still relatively rare. But breast cancer is not rare — it is the most common cancer in women worldwide. In the United States, one in eight women will be diagnosed with breast cancer in her lifetime. For South Asian women, whose baseline risk is slightly lower than white women but rising, a threefold increase from insomnia moves the needle meaningfully.

## From Awareness to Action

Sleep medicine experts say the first step is reframing insomnia from a nuisance to a health risk on par with smoking or obesity. Just as a doctor would flag a patient's smoking status in a cancer risk assessment, persistent insomnia should trigger a similar conversation.

For South Asian families, this means taking sleep complaints seriously — especially from women who may downplay their own needs. If someone in your family has been struggling with sleep for more than three months, it qualifies as chronic insomnia under clinical guidelines and warrants a conversation with a doctor, not a suggestion to drink more turmeric milk.

Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, known as CBT-I, is the gold-standard treatment and has been shown to be more effective than medication in the long term. It is available through telehealth, which makes it accessible even for women with limited daytime availability. Several apps now offer guided CBT-I programs that can be completed in six to eight weeks.

The broader takeaway from ASCO 2026 is that cancer prevention is no longer just about diet, exercise, and screenings. Sleep belongs in that conversation — and for South Asian women juggling two time zones, two cultures, and too many responsibilities, it may be the single most modifiable risk factor they are not addressing.
